title: Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Shri Piyush Goyal Chairs India-Japan Industry Roundtable on Semiconductors and Artificial Intelligence in Tokyo
subtitle: Shri Piyush Goyal Holds Bilateral Meeting with Japan’s Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry; Both Ministers Agree to Accelerate Review of CEPA
body_text:
Union Minister of Commerce and Industry, Shri Piyush Goyal, today chaired a roundtable with leading Japanese and Indian industry representatives on Semiconductors and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Tokyo, underlining the growing importance of these sunrise sectors in strengthening India-Japan economic and technological cooperation.
Shri Goyal highlighted that Semiconductors and AI are emerging as key areas of cooperation and constitute an important pillar of the economic security partnership envisaged by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi during the Annual Summit. He assured the participating industry representatives of the Government of India’s wholehearted support in deepening and expanding collaboration between India and Japan in these strategic sectors.
The Minister highlighted the rapidly expanding opportunities in India’s semiconductor sector, with domestic semiconductor demand projected to reach USD 150 billion by 2032. He outlined the Government’s comprehensive semiconductor strategy covering chip design, semiconductor machinery and materials, fabrication, ATMP/OSAT, research and development, and talent development. He also highlighted the Government’s commitment of USD 10 billion under Semicon India 1.0 and an additional USD 15 billion under Semicon India 2.0 to catalyse large-scale investments and build a comprehensive semiconductor ecosystem in the country.
Shri Goyal emphasised the significant potential for combining India’s vast pool of skilled and talented professionals with Japan’s advanced technology, engineering capabilities and industrial expertise. He noted that such complementarities can create new opportunities for investment, innovation, manufacturing and technology partnerships between the two countries.
The roundtable was attended by representatives of around 21 leading Japanese companies, including Tokyo Electron, Daifuku, Preferred Networks, ABEJA, MinebeaMitsumi, Tanaka Precious Metals Technologies, Fujifilm Holdings, Toray Industries, Nippon Express Holdings, Mizuho Financial Group, Kyocera Corporation, Fuji Electric, TOK, Air Water Inc., ROHM, Tomoegawa Corporation, MUFG Bank Ltd., NEC Corporation, Yamaya Electronics, ANA Trading and JETRO. The roundtable also saw participation from various Indian business chambers and business delegations.
The participating Japanese companies expressed confidence in the growing opportunities in India’s semiconductor and AI sectors and reaffirmed their commitment to Make in India, Design in India and Develop in India. The companies also briefed the Minister on their operations, capabilities and project execution in the relevant sectors.
Responding to suggestions and concerns raised by Japanese industry representatives, Shri Goyal assured that the Government of India would proactively address the issues raised. He emphasised that India is fully cognisant of the significant potential of the India-Japan partnership in these strategic sectors and will proactively engage with industry through the Embassy of India in Tokyo and the concerned Ministries and Departments in New Delhi to facilitate fruitful outcomes in a fast-tracked manner.
Earlier, Shri Goyal held a bilateral meeting with Japan’s Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry, H.E. Mr. Akazawa Ryosei, on 25 August 2026 in Tokyo.
During the meeting, the two Ministers took stock of bilateral economic cooperation, including bilateral trade and investment, and discussed the need to accelerate the review of the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) to make it more forward-looking and responsive to emerging economic opportunities.
The Ministers also discussed bilateral cooperation in new and emerging sectors, next-generation industries, manufacturing, technology and innovation. They noted the steady progress towards achieving the target of JPY 10 trillion in private investment from Japan to India, further strengthening the India-Japan Special Strategic and Global Partnership.
Delighted to meet Mr. Akazawa Ryosei, Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry of Japan. We discussed ways to further strengthen India-Japan trade, investment and industrial cooperation, building on the momentum of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s visit to India for the 16th… pic.twitter.com/j6hpInWuHz — Piyush Goyal (@PiyushGoyal) August 25, 2026
***
Abhishek Dayal/ Ishita Biswas

enrichment.summary: Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal chaired an India-Japan industry roundtable on semiconductors and AI in Tokyo on 25 August 2026, attended by around 21 Japanese companies and Indian business delegations. He also held a bilateral meeting with Japan's METI Minister Akazawa Ryosei, where both sides agreed to accelerate the review of the India-Japan Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) and discussed progress towards the JPY 10 trillion Japanese private investment target in India.
enrichment.context:
India's semiconductor push is anchored in the Semicon India Programme, launched in 2021 with an initial outlay (referred to here as Semicon India 1.0) to build fabrication, ATMP/OSAT, and design ecosystems through incentives to companies like Micron, Tata Electronics, and others. The mention of an additional USD 15 billion tranche (Semicon India 2.0) signals an expansion of this strategy amid global chip supply-chain realignment and India's ambition to become a major electronics and semiconductor manufacturing hub, with domestic demand projected to reach USD 150 billion by 2032. Japan, a global leader in semiconductor materials and manufacturing equipment (companies like Tokyo Electron, ROHM, Kyocera), is a natural partner given its Chip Act and interest in diversifying supply chains away from over-reliance on Taiwan and China.

The India-Japan Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), in force since 2011, has long been criticised for underperforming relative to its potential, with India running a trade deficit and limited utilisation of tariff concessions by exporters. A review of CEPA to make it more responsive to emerging sectors like semiconductors, AI, and green technology fits into the broader India-Japan Special Strategic and Global Partnership, reinforced by the JPY 5 trillion (now aiming for JPY 10 trillion) investment pledge from Japan to India, and follows on from Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's summit visit to India referenced in the release.

prelims_questions.question: The 'Semicon India Programme' primarily aims to support which of the following?
options: Development of India's semiconductor design, fabrication, and ATMP/OSAT ecosystem
Setting up of new IT parks in tier-2 cities
Expansion of India's telecom spectrum allocation
prelims_questions.explanation: The Semicon India Programme, referenced in the release with USD 10 billion (1.0) and an additional USD 15 billion (2.0) commitment, supports chip design, semiconductor machinery/materials, fabrication, ATMP/OSAT, R&D, and talent development.

prelims_questions.question: The Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), whose review India and Japan agreed to accelerate, has been in force since which year?
prelims_questions.explanation: The India-Japan CEPA came into force in 2011 and governs bilateral trade in goods, services, and investment between the two countries.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the strategic importance of semiconductor manufacturing for India's economic security and examine how international partnerships, such as with Japan, can help build a resilient domestic semiconductor ecosystem.
Evaluate the significance of periodic review of trade agreements like the India-Japan CEPA in adapting to emerging sectors such as semiconductors and artificial intelligence.

study_notes.reason: The release's real value lies in situating India-Japan cooperation within economic security, semiconductor strategy, and CEPA review dynamics rather than in any single testable fact, though a few scheme-figure facts are worth noting.

prelims.point: Semicon India Programme: USD 10 billion committed under 'Semicon India 1.0'; an additional USD 15 billion announced under 'Semicon India 2.0'
prelims.why_important: Specific dollar figures for phases of a flagship scheme are classic PIB-based prelims fodder.

prelims.point: India-Japan CEPA (Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement) has been in force since 2011 and is currently under review
prelims.why_important: Aspirants should know the existence and vintage of India's key bilateral trade agreements and their current status.

prelims.point: India's domestic semiconductor demand is projected to reach USD 150 billion by 2032
prelims.why_important: A quantified projection that could appear as a factual statement in a statement-based question on India's semiconductor sector.

mains.point: Semiconductors and AI are being framed as pillars of an 'economic security partnership' between India and Japan, reflecting global supply-chain realignment away from Taiwan/China concentration
mains.analytical_use: Useful for questions on how technology cooperation is being used as an instrument of strategic partnership and supply-chain diversification in India's foreign policy.

mains.point: Government's comprehensive semiconductor strategy spans chip design, machinery/materials, fabrication, ATMP/OSAT, R&D and talent development, aiming to build a full ecosystem rather than isolated units
mains.analytical_use: Can be used to discuss whether India's semiconductor policy is building an integrated ecosystem or remains fragmented, relevant to 'Discuss India's strategy for semiconductor self-reliance' type questions.

mains.point: India-Japan CEPA has historically underperformed relative to its potential, with limited utilisation of tariff concessions and a persistent trade deficit for India, prompting the current push for review
mains.analytical_use: Supports analytical questions on why India's FTAs/CEPAs often fail to deliver expected trade gains and what reforms are needed to make them more effective.

mains.point: Progress towards the JPY 10 trillion Japanese private investment target signals deepening economic interdependence but raises questions about absorption capacity and implementation on the Indian side
mains.analytical_use: Useful for 'way forward' sections discussing India's capacity to convert investment pledges into on-ground project execution.

mains.point: Japanese industry raised concerns/suggestions during the roundtable, indicating persistent ease-of-doing-business or regulatory friction points despite high-level political commitment
mains.theme: Ease of doing business for foreign investors
mains.analytical_use: Can be cited as evidence of implementation gaps between government intent and ground-level investor experience in answers on FDI facilitation.
